# Least Squares as Projection


Suppose the columns of $\bA$ describe the responses available to a model. Every prediction has the form $\bA\bx$ and therefore lies in the column space of $\bA$. If an observation $\bb$ lies outside that space, no choice of parameters can fit it exactly. Least squares asks for the point in the column space closest to the observation.


The choice of norm therefore matters. Euclidean least squares regards squared orthogonal distance as the loss. A different norm expresses a different meaning of error and generally leads to a different estimator.


## The Geometric Problem


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Definition: Linear Least-Squares Problem
For $\bA\in\fR^{m\times n}$ and $\bb\in\fR^m$, the linear least-squares problem is
$$
\begin{align}
\min_{\bx\in\fR^n}\|\bA\bx-\bb\|_2^2
    =
    \min_{\bx\in\fR^n}
    \sum_{i=1}^m
    \left(\sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}x_j-b_i\right)^2.
\end{align}
$$
The residual associated with $\bx$ is $\br(\bx)=\bb-\bA\bx$.
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Theorem: Orthogonal Characterization and Normal Equations
A vector $\widehat{\bx}$ is a least-squares minimizer if and only if its residual is orthogonal to every column of $\bA$:
$$
\begin{align}
\br=\bb-\bA\widehat{\bx}
    \perp\mathcal{R}(\bA).
\end{align}
$$
Equivalently,
$$
\begin{align}
\bA^T\br=\bzero,
    \qquad
    \bA^T\bA\widehat{\bx}=\bA^T\bb.
\end{align}
$$
These are the **normal equations**. A minimizer is unique exactly when the columns of $\bA$ are linearly independent.
:::


::: {.callout-tip icon=false collapse=true}
## Proof
Decompose $\bb-\bA\bx$ by inserting the candidate fitted vector $\bA\widehat{\bx}$:
$$
\begin{align}
\bb-\bA\bx
    &= (\bb-\bA\widehat{\bx}) + \bA(\widehat{\bx}-\bx).
\end{align}
$$
If $\bb-\bA\widehat{\bx}\perp\mathcal{R}(\bA)$, then since $\bA(\widehat{\bx}-\bx)\in\mathcal{R}(\bA)$, the two summands are orthogonal:
$$
\begin{align}
(\bb-\bA\widehat{\bx})^T\bA(\widehat{\bx}-\bx) = 0.
\end{align}
$$
The Pythagorean identity therefore yields
$$
\begin{align}
\|\bb-\bA\bx\|_2^2
    &= \|(\bb-\bA\widehat{\bx}) + \bA(\widehat{\bx}-\bx)\|_2^2 \\
    &= \|\bb-\bA\widehat{\bx}\|_2^2 + \|\bA(\widehat{\bx}-\bx)\|_2^2
    \ge \|\bb-\bA\widehat{\bx}\|_2^2.
\end{align}
$$
Equality holds if and only if $\|\bA(\widehat{\bx}-\bx)\|_2^2=0$, meaning $\bA(\widehat{\bx}-\bx)=\bzero$. Thus $\widehat{\bx}$ minimizes the residual norm.

Conversely, if $\widehat{\bx}$ is a minimizer, define for any $\bv\in\fR^n$ and $t\in\fR$ the scalar function
$$
\begin{align}
\phi(t)
    &= \|\bb-\bA(\widehat{\bx}+t\bv)\|_2^2 \\
    &= \|\br - t\bA\bv\|_2^2 \\
    &= \|\br\|_2^2 - 2t\,\bv^T\bA^T\br + t^2\|\bA\bv\|_2^2,
\end{align}
$$
where $\br=\bb-\bA\widehat{\bx}$. Because $\phi$ has a global minimum at $t=0$,
$$
\begin{align}
\phi'(0) = -2\bv^T\bA^T\br = 0
    \quad\text{for all }\bv\in\fR^n.
\end{align}
$$
Choosing $\bv = \be_j$ for $j=1,...,n$ gives $\bA^T\br=\bzero$, which means $\br\perp\mathcal{R}(\bA)$. Expanding $\bA^T(\bb-\bA\widehat{\bx})=\bzero$ yields the normal equations
$$
\begin{align}
\bA^T\bA\widehat{\bx}=\bA^T\bb.
\end{align}
$$

For uniqueness, suppose $\widehat{\bx}_1$ and $\widehat{\bx}_2$ are both minimizers. Then $\bA(\widehat{\bx}_1-\widehat{\bx}_2)=\bzero$, so $\widehat{\bx}_1-\widehat{\bx}_2\in\mathcal{N}(\bA)$. When $\bA$ has full column rank, $\mathcal{N}(\bA)=\{\bzero\}$, forcing $\widehat{\bx}_1=\widehat{\bx}_2$. If $\bz\in\mathcal{N}(\bA)\setminus\{\bzero\}$, then $\bA(\widehat{\bx}+\bz)=\bA\widehat{\bx}$, so $\widehat{\bx}+\bz$ is also a minimizer.
:::


::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Remark
**(Normal Equations via Differentiation)**
For $f(\bx)=\frac12\|\bA\bx-\bb\|_2^2$, the gradient is $\nabla f(\bx)=\bA^T(\bA\bx-\bb)$. Setting $\nabla f(\bx)=\bzero$ recovers $\bA^T\bA\bx=\bA^T\bb$. The Pythagorean argument reveals why the condition is sufficient and geometrically necessary.
:::


::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Remark
**(Conditioning of Normal Equations)**
When $\bA$ has full column rank, $\bA^T\bA$ is SPD because
$$
\begin{align}
\bx^T\bA^T\bA\bx=\|\bA\bx\|_2^2>0
\end{align}
$$
for nonzero $\bx$. This proves that the normal equations have a unique solution.
:::


The normal equations replace the rectangular problem by a square one, but forming $\bA^T\bA$ hides the geometry and worsens sensitivity. QR instead chooses orthonormal coordinates adapted to the column space.


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Theorem: Least-Squares Solution by QR
Let $\bA\in\fR^{m\times n}$ have full column rank and thin QR factorization $\bA=\bQ_1\bR_1$. Then the unique least-squares solution is obtained from
$$
\begin{align}
\bR_1\widehat{\bx}=\bQ_1^T\bb.
\end{align}
$$
The fitted vector and residual are
$$
\begin{align}
\widehat{\bb}=\bQ_1\bQ_1^T\bb,
    \qquad
    \br=(\bI-\bQ_1\bQ_1^T)\bb.
\end{align}
$$
:::


::: {.callout-tip icon=false collapse=true}
## Proof
Let $\bQ = (\bQ_1  \bQ_2)\in\fR^{m\times m}$ be orthogonal, where $\bQ_1\in\fR^{m\times n}$ and $\bQ_2\in\fR^{m\times (m-n)}$. Since $\bQ^T\bQ=\bI$, the Euclidean norm is orthogonally invariant:
$$
\begin{align}
\|\bA\bx-\bb\|_2^2
    &= \|\bQ^T(\bA\bx-\bb)\|_2^2 \\
    &= \left\|
    \begin{pmatrix}\bQ_1^T\\\bQ_2^T\end{pmatrix}(\bQ_1\bR_1\bx - \bb)
    \right\|_2^2 \\
    &= \left\|
    \begin{pmatrix}\bR_1\bx - \bQ_1^T\bb\\ -\bQ_2^T\bb\end{pmatrix}
    \right\|_2^2 \\
    &= \|\bR_1\bx-\bQ_1^T\bb\|_2^2 + \|\bQ_2^T\bb\|_2^2.
\end{align}
$$
The second term $\|\bQ_2^T\bb\|_2^2$ is fixed and independent of $\bx$. Because $\bA$ has full column rank, $\bR_1$ is non-singular, and setting $\bR_1\widehat{\bx}=\bQ_1^T\bb$ reduces the first term to zero, attaining the minimum value $\|\bQ_2^T\bb\|_2^2$. The fitted vector and residual follow:
$$
\begin{align}
\widehat{\bb} &= \bA\widehat{\bx} = \bQ_1\bR_1(\bR_1^{-1}\bQ_1^T\bb) = \bQ_1\bQ_1^T\bb, \\
    \br &= \bb - \widehat{\bb} = (\bI - \bQ_1\bQ_1^T)\bb.
\end{align}
$$
:::


::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Remark
**(Geometry vs. Conditioning in Householder QR)**
For a matrix with full column rank, the referenced result proves $\kappa_2(\bA^T\bA)=\kappa_2(\bA)^2$. Householder QR avoids forming $\bA^T\bA$ and is the safer dense default. The normal equations remain useful when special structure, cost, or repeated updates make the trade worthwhile.
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Example
Fitting $y=c_0+c_1t$ to $(0,1)$, $(1,2)$, and $(2,4)$ gives
$$
\begin{align}
\bA=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},
    \qquad
    \bb=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\4\end{pmatrix}.
\end{align}
$$
The solution is $c_0=5/6$ and $c_1=3/2$. The residual is orthogonal to both the constant column and the time column. Hence its entries sum to zero and have zero first moment with respect to the sample times.
:::
## Rank-Deficient Problems


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Theorem: All Minimizers and the Minimum-Norm Choice
Let $\widehat{\bx}$ be any least-squares minimizer. Then every minimizer has the form
$$
\begin{align}
\widehat{\bx}+\bz,
    \qquad \bz\in\mathcal{N}(\bA).
\end{align}
$$
Among them there is exactly one vector of smallest Euclidean norm. It is characterized by
$$
\begin{align}
\widehat{\bx}_{\min}\perp\mathcal{N}(\bA),
    \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad
    \widehat{\bx}_{\min}\in\mathcal{R}(\bA^T).
\end{align}
$$
:::


::: {.callout-tip icon=false collapse=true}
## Proof
Let $\widehat{\bx}$ be any minimizer. For any $\bz\in\mathcal{N}(\bA)$, $\bA(\widehat{\bx}+\bz)=\bA\widehat{\bx}$, so $\widehat{\bx}+\bz$ is also a minimizer. Conversely, if $\bx'$ is any minimizer, then $\bA\bx'=\bA\widehat{\bx}$ by uniqueness of the orthogonal projection $\widehat{\bb}$, which gives $\bA(\bx'-\widehat{\bx})=\bzero$, so $\bx'-\widehat{\bx}\in\mathcal{N}(\bA)$.

Every vector decomposes uniquely as $\bx = \bx_{\perp} + \bx_0$ with $\bx_0\in\mathcal{N}(\bA)$ and $\bx_{\perp}\in\mathcal{N}(\bA)^\perp$. For any minimizer $\widehat{\bx} + \bz$, we have $\bz\in\mathcal{N}(\bA)$, so
$$
\begin{align}
\|\widehat{\bx}+\bz\|_2^2
    &= \|(\widehat{\bx}_{\perp} + \widehat{\bx}_0) + \bz\|_2^2 \\
    &= \|\widehat{\bx}_{\perp} + (\widehat{\bx}_0 + \bz)\|_2^2 \\
    &= \|\widehat{\bx}_{\perp}\|_2^2 + \|\widehat{\bx}_0 + \bz\|_2^2
    \ge \|\widehat{\bx}_{\perp}\|_2^2.
\end{align}
$$
The minimum is attained uniquely when $\bz = -\widehat{\bx}_0$, which yields $\widehat{\bx}_{\min} = \widehat{\bx}_{\perp}\in\mathcal{N}(\bA)^\perp$. By the fundamental theorem of linear algebra, $\mathcal{N}(\bA)^\perp = \mathcal{R}(\bA^T)$.
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Definition: Tikhonov Regularization
For $\lambda>0$, Tikhonov or ridge regularization solves
$$
\begin{align}
\min_{\bx}
    \left(\|\bA\bx-\bb\|_2^2+\lambda\|\bx\|_2^2\right).
\end{align}
$$
It trades residual fit against parameter size. The problem is equivalently the augmented least-squares problem
$$
\begin{align}
\min_{\bx}
    \left\|
    \begin{pmatrix}\bA\\\sqrt{\lambda}\bI\end{pmatrix}\bx
    -
    \begin{pmatrix}\bb\\\bzero\end{pmatrix}
    \right\|_2^2,
\end{align}
$$
and its normal equations are
$$
\begin{align}
(\bA^T\bA+\lambda\bI)\bx=\bA^T\bb.
\end{align}
$$
:::


::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Remark
**(Interpretation of Regularization)**
Regularization also adds a modeling assumption. Among models with similar fit, it prefers smaller parameter vectors. Whether that assumption is scientifically appropriate depends on the meaning and scaling of the parameters. the referenced result identifies the directions that regularization damps and the amount by which each is damped.
:::


## Exercises


::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## Exercise

1. **Derive.**  Starting only from the orthogonal decomposition theorem, rederive the normal equations and prove both directions of the referenced result. Do not use derivatives.

1. **Compute.**  Fit a parabola $y=c_0+c_1t+c_2t^2$ to $(-1,1)$, $(0,0)$, $(1,1)$, and $(2,5)$ using thin QR. Verify orthogonality of the residual against each column to working precision.

1. **Explore.**  Construct two almost parallel columns in $\fR^3$. Compare the condition and numerical orthogonality of solutions obtained from normal equations, modified Gram--Schmidt QR, and Householder QR as the angle between the columns decreases.

1. **Derive.**  Suppose $\bA\bx=\bb$ is consistent but underdetermined. Prove that the minimum-norm solution is orthogonal to the null space. Explain why adding any invisible null-space component increases the norm without changing the data fit.

1. **Derive.**  Let $\bW$ be SPD. Weighted least squares minimizes $\|\bA\bx-\bb\|_{\bW}^2$. Prove that the residual is $\bW$-orthogonal to $\mathcal{R}(\bA)$ and derive $\bA^T\bW\bA\bx=\bA^T\bW\bb$. Explain what statistical or physical information the weight matrix expresses.

1. **Explore.**  Rescale one column of a data matrix by $10^6$. The set of fitted vectors does not change if its coefficient is rescaled inversely, but the ridge penalty does. Explain why regularization cannot be interpreted independently of units.

:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Further reading
Meyer develops the geometry and algebra with unusual clarity [@meyer2000]. Golub and Van Loan give the algorithmic treatment, while Higham explains what finite precision changes [@golubvanloan2013; @higham2002]. Trefethen and Bau provide a concise bridge between the geometry and the computation [@trefethenbau1997].
:::
